title: How the Node.js Runtime Works
description: Explain what V8, libuv, the operating system, and the JavaScript thread each do.

blocks.title: How the Node.js Runtime Works
blocks.content:
V8 executes JavaScript. Node.js exposes host APIs for files, networking, processes, and timers. libuv coordinates the event loop and a pool used by selected operations such as many file-system calls. Network readiness is commonly handled through operating-system facilities. When work completes, Node schedules the JavaScript callback on its event loop.

A service can handle many requests while waiting for I/O, but CPU work on the main thread delays every callback in that process. The example starts a file read and logs before awaiting it. The read runs through an asynchronous API, and the result is delivered when the event loop can resume JavaScript.
keyPoints: Measure time spent running JavaScript separately from time awaiting dependencies.
The main event-loop thread runs application callbacks. Worker threads and the libuv pool have different owners and solve different problems.

blocks.title: Run as runtime.mjs
blocks.explanation: The main event-loop thread runs application callbacks. Worker threads and the libuv pool have different owners and solve different problems.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Why can one Node process handle multiple HTTP requests concurrently?
blocks.answer: Each request can yield while waiting for I/O, so the event loop can run callbacks for other requests. JavaScript callbacks on the same event-loop thread execute one at a time.
blocks.explanation: The main event-loop thread runs application callbacks. Worker threads and the libuv pool have different owners and solve different problems.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Does adding async to a large CPU-bound function move its work off the event loop?
blocks.answer: No. Its synchronous body still executes on the current thread. An await yields only after reaching an awaited operation, and the continuation also runs on that thread.
hints: Locate where the computation runs.
blocks.explanation:
The main event-loop thread runs application callbacks. Worker threads and the libuv pool have different owners and solve different problems.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/dont-block-the-event-loop)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: Requests become slow only when a report is generated. How do you confirm and fix the cause?
blocks.answer: Compare main-thread CPU and event-loop delay for runs with and without the report. Profile the report path. Move independent CPU work to a bounded worker pool or a background service and measure p95 latency under concurrent traffic.
blocks.explanation: Measure time spent running JavaScript separately from time awaiting dependencies.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Equating async APIs with CPU parallelism.
blocks.whyItHappens: The keyword changes how the function returns results, so it is easy to mistake the promise interface for a change in executor.
blocks.correctApproach: Measure time spent running JavaScript separately from time awaiting dependencies.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Measure time spent running JavaScript separately from time awaiting dependencies.

The main event-loop thread runs application callbacks. Worker threads and the libuv pool have different owners and solve different problems.

blocks.content:
Explain what V8, libuv, the operating system, and the JavaScript thread each do. Each request can yield while waiting for I/O, so the event loop can run callbacks for other requests. JavaScript callbacks on the same event-loop thread execute one at a time.

title: Event Loop, Microtasks, and Timers
description: Predict execution order within a known context and explain timer delays and starvation.

blocks.title: Event Loop, Microtasks, and Timers
blocks.content:
Timers specify a minimum delay. The event loop can run their callbacks later due to other work. I/O callbacks generally run through the poll phase, and setImmediate callbacks run in the check phase. Inside an I/O callback, an immediate normally runs before a zero-delay timer scheduled there. Ordering between those two at top level is context dependent.

Promise reactions and queueMicrotask work share the microtask queue. Node maintains a separate next-tick queue. In CommonJS top-level execution it drains before microtasks, while top-level ES module evaluation itself runs in a microtask and can produce a different order. Recursive next-tick or microtask scheduling can starve I/O.
keyPoints: Calculate expiry from a timestamp and use scheduling only to trigger another check.
For ordering questions, state the module format and callback context before predicting an output.

blocks.explanation: For ordering questions, state the module format and callback context before predicting an output.

blocks.title: Predict the output
blocks.question: What lines print when running ordering.cjs?
blocks.answer:
start
end
next tick
promise
microtask
blocks.explanation: Synchronous code runs first. At this CommonJS top-level boundary the next-tick queue drains before V8's shared microtask queue.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: How are timers different from promise callbacks?
blocks.answer: Timer callbacks become eligible after their delay and execute in an event-loop phase. Promise reactions run through the microtask queue after the current synchronous work completes.
blocks.explanation: For ordering questions, state the module format and callback context before predicting an output.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Is the observed top-level CommonJS order guaranteed if you rename ordering.cjs to ordering.mjs?
blocks.answer: No. The ES module is evaluated through the microtask machinery. For this exact example, start and end still come first, then promise, microtask, and next tick.

blocks.explanation:
For ordering questions, state the module format and callback context before predicting an output.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/learn/asynchronous-work/event-loop-timers-and-nexttick)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: A timer set for 100 ms regularly fires after 700 ms. What do you measure?
blocks.answer: Measure event-loop delay and CPU alongside request latency. Profile synchronous callbacks and check container CPU throttling and GC pauses before changing the timer interval.
blocks.explanation: Calculate expiry from a timestamp and use scheduling only to trigger another check.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Using setTimeout as a precise clock.
blocks.whyItHappens: The specified delay controls eligibility. Existing work can delay the event loop's opportunity to run the callback.
blocks.correctApproach: Calculate expiry from a timestamp and use scheduling only to trigger another check.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Calculate expiry from a timestamp and use scheduling only to trigger another check.

For ordering questions, state the module format and callback context before predicting an output.

Predict execution order within a known context and explain timer delays and starvation. Timer callbacks become eligible after their delay and execute in an event-loop phase. Promise reactions run through the microtask queue after the current synchronous work completes.

title: ES Modules, CommonJS, and Package Exports
description: Choose a module format explicitly and design a stable package entry point.

blocks.title: ES Modules, CommonJS, and Package Exports
blocks.content:
Use .mjs or .cjs for an explicit file-level format, or set the package type for .js files. In ES modules, relative imports normally include extensions. CommonJS uses require and module.exports. Dynamic import is asynchronous and can load from either module system.

The exports field defines supported package entry points and can select conditional entries. Type declarations and JavaScript entry points must agree. Publishing separate CommonJS and ESM implementations can introduce separate singleton instances when both are loaded in a process.
keyPoints: Install the packed artifact in clean ESM and CommonJS fixtures when you support both.
Combining import and require conditions needs integration tests because the public resolution paths can diverge.

blocks.title: Example package.json
blocks.explanation: Combining import and require conditions needs integration tests because the public resolution paths can diverge.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What does exports protect in package.json?
blocks.answer: It defines the package subpaths accessible through normal package resolution. This creates a public API boundary. It is not a sandbox that restricts local filesystem access.
blocks.explanation: Combining import and require conditions needs integration tests because the public resolution paths can diverge.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Can a CommonJS consumer always require an ES module that works with import?
blocks.answer: No. Modern Node versions can require compatible synchronous ESM, but a graph that uses top-level await requires asynchronous loading via import(). Older Node versions have different support.
hints: Check whether the entire module graph can evaluate synchronously.
blocks.explanation:
Combining import and require conditions needs integration tests because the public resolution paths can diverge.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/api/packages.html)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: A library adds exports and existing clients fail on deep imports. How do you roll out the change?
blocks.answer: Inventory imported subpaths. Expose supported compatibility paths, migrate consumers to public exports, and test installed tarballs in supported Node versions. Treat removal of an existing public entry as a breaking change.
blocks.explanation: Install the packed artifact in clean ESM and CommonJS fixtures when you support both.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Testing resolution only inside the monorepo.
blocks.whyItHappens: Workspace tooling can make files visible through links or aliases that consumers do not have after installing the published package.
blocks.correctApproach: Install the packed artifact in clean ESM and CommonJS fixtures when you support both.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Install the packed artifact in clean ESM and CommonJS fixtures when you support both.

Combining import and require conditions needs integration tests because the public resolution paths can diverge.

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.content:
Choose a module format explicitly and design a stable package entry point. It defines the package subpaths accessible through normal package resolution. This creates a public API boundary. It is not a sandbox that restricts local filesystem access.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/api/packages.html)

title: npm Lockfiles and Reproducible Installs
description: Explain dependency ranges, lockfiles, and predictable CI installs.

blocks.title: npm Lockfiles and Reproducible Installs
blocks.content:
The package manifest declares acceptable dependency versions and project scripts. The lockfile records the resolved tree so coworkers and build systems can install it consistently. npm ci expects the manifest and lockfile to agree and replaces the existing install tree.

Use a consistent Node and npm version in CI. Lockfiles cannot guarantee identical outputs when native binaries, operating systems, scripts, or environment settings differ. Review intentional lockfile diffs and pin critical toolchain dependencies where appropriate.
keyPoints: Keep toolchain versions explicit and validate the project using clean installs in CI.
Use the same lockfile and package-manager version when comparing clean installs across machines.

blocks.title: Example CI command sequence
blocks.code:
node --version
npm --version
npm ci
npm test
blocks.explanation: Use the same lockfile and package-manager version when comparing clean installs across machines.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: When should you use npm ci instead of npm install?
blocks.answer: Use npm ci for a clean, lockfile-driven install in CI. Use npm install when intentionally changing dependencies or updating the lockfile.
blocks.explanation: Use the same lockfile and package-manager version when comparing clean installs across machines.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Will npm ci repair a lockfile that no longer agrees with package.json?
blocks.answer: No. It exits with an error. Update the lockfile as part of the intended dependency change, review the result, and commit both files.
hints: Decide whether the command is allowed to rewrite the lockfile.
blocks.explanation:
Use the same lockfile and package-manager version when comparing clean installs across machines.

[Further reading](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npm-ci)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: The build works on a developer laptop but fails loading a native addon in CI. What do you compare?
blocks.answer: Compare Node, npm, operating system and architecture, supported prebuilt binaries, and install logs. Reproduce using the same environment as CI before changing package versions.
blocks.explanation: Keep toolchain versions explicit and validate the project using clean installs in CI.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Deleting the lockfile to fix a single machine's stale installation.
blocks.whyItHappens: A local dependency problem can persist in the generated install tree even when the committed resolution is correct.
blocks.correctApproach: Keep toolchain versions explicit and validate the project using clean installs in CI.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Keep toolchain versions explicit and validate the project using clean installs in CI.

Use the same lockfile and package-manager version when comparing clean installs across machines.

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.content:
Explain dependency ranges, lockfiles, and predictable CI installs. Use npm ci for a clean, lockfile-driven install in CI. Use npm install when intentionally changing dependencies or updating the lockfile.

[Further reading](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npm-ci)

title: Promises, Async Errors, and Concurrency Limits
description: Handle rejected promises, distinguish batch failure policies, and bound fan-out.

blocks.title: Promises, Async Errors, and Concurrency Limits
blocks.content:
Await turns rejection into a throw at the await point, where a try/catch can add context or translate it. An error thrown in a separate callback is outside an earlier synchronous catch. Return or await asynchronous work so its owner can observe failure.

Promise.all rejects when one input rejects. Operations already started keep running unless their APIs support cancellation and the caller requests it. Promise.allSettled keeps every result. Batch or pool scheduling controls how many jobs start concurrently.
keyPoints: Use a for-of loop for sequential execution or an explicit bounded scheduler for concurrent execution.
Pick the scheduling limit and the result policy independently. Batch boundaries in this example can leave capacity idle while the slowest task finishes.

blocks.title: Run as batches.mjs
blocks.explanation: Pick the scheduling limit and the result policy independently. Batch boundaries in this example can leave capacity idle while the slowest task finishes.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: When should you use Promise.allSettled?
blocks.answer: Use it when each operation has value independently and you need to report individual outcomes. For dependent operations that require every result, a combined failure may be the correct response.
blocks.explanation: Pick the scheduling limit and the result policy independently. Batch boundaries in this example can leave capacity idle while the slowest task finishes.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Does Promise.all limit how many tasks start or cancel siblings after a rejection?
blocks.answer: Neither. Calling functions during map starts their operations before Promise.all observes the resulting promises. Bound the launch rate, and use an AbortSignal only where the operations support it.
hints: Separate launching work from observing promises.
blocks.explanation:
Pick the scheduling limit and the result policy independently. Batch boundaries in this example can leave capacity idle while the slowest task finishes.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/discover-promises-in-nodejs)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: A bulk task starts 10,000 database requests and exhausts the connection pool. What changes?
blocks.answer: Introduce a bounded queue with a concurrency limit aligned to the pool and system load. Track waiting time, impose a deadline, and decide whether partial failures should be recorded or fail the job.
blocks.explanation: Use a for-of loop for sequential execution or an explicit bounded scheduler for concurrent execution.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Using forEach with async callbacks and assuming the enclosing function waits.
blocks.whyItHappens: Array.forEach discards the callback's return value, including the promise returned by an async callback.
blocks.correctApproach: Use a for-of loop for sequential execution or an explicit bounded scheduler for concurrent execution.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Use a for-of loop for sequential execution or an explicit bounded scheduler for concurrent execution.

Pick the scheduling limit and the result policy independently. Batch boundaries in this example can leave capacity idle while the slowest task finishes.

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.content:
Handle rejected promises, distinguish batch failure policies, and bound fan-out. Use it when each operation has value independently and you need to report individual outcomes. For dependent operations that require every result, a combined failure may be the correct response.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/discover-promises-in-nodejs)

title: EventEmitter and Listener Lifecycle
description: Use synchronous event dispatch and manage listener ownership.

blocks.title: EventEmitter and Listener Lifecycle
blocks.content:
EventEmitter calls listeners synchronously in registration order when emit is called. Returning a promise from a listener does not make ordinary emit await it. A special error event without a listener normally throws.

Use once for a one-shot subscription and off for explicit ownership. Register event listeners before an event can fire. A long-lived emitter can retain objects through closures if cleanup never runs.
keyPoints: Test that listener counts return to their baseline after cancellation and completion.
For async listeners, decide where rejected promises are handled and how the emitter owner learns about completion.

blocks.title: Run as events.mjs
blocks.explanation: For async listeners, decide where rejected promises are handled and how the emitter owner learns about completion.

blocks.title: Predict the output
blocks.question: Which lines print from the two done events?
blocks.answer: completed A
blocks.explanation: The once listener is removed when the first emission runs. There is no done listener left for the second emission.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What is the difference between on and once?
blocks.answer: on registers a listener until removed. once removes its listener when it fires, before invoking the original callback.
blocks.explanation: For async listeners, decide where rejected promises are handled and how the emitter owner learns about completion.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Does emit await an async listener before invoking the next listener?
blocks.answer: No. It invokes listeners synchronously in order. The async listener runs up to its first await and returns a promise immediately. Use an explicit awaitable API when completion must be known.
hints: Look at what emit returns and who owns the promise.
blocks.explanation:
For async listeners, decide where rejected promises are handled and how the emitter owner learns about completion.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/api/events.html)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: A warning about too many listeners appears after each map refresh in a server-side service. What do you inspect?
blocks.answer: Find which code attaches the listeners, verify count across repeated refreshes, and remove the same callback during lifecycle cleanup. Increase the listener limit only when the subscriber count is intentional and bounded.
blocks.explanation: Test that listener counts return to their baseline after cancellation and completion.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Quieting a listener warning without identifying ownership.
blocks.whyItHappens: The listener threshold is a warning signal. Changing it does not remove leaked callbacks or their closures.
blocks.correctApproach: Test that listener counts return to their baseline after cancellation and completion.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Test that listener counts return to their baseline after cancellation and completion.

For async listeners, decide where rejected promises are handled and how the emitter owner learns about completion.

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.content:
Use synchronous event dispatch and manage listener ownership. on registers a listener until removed. once removes its listener when it fires, before invoking the original callback.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/api/events.html)

title: AbortSignal, Deadlines, and Cancellation
description: Propagate request deadlines into asynchronous dependencies.

blocks.title: AbortSignal, Deadlines, and Cancellation
blocks.content:
A deadline caps the time available to an operation. AbortSignal communicates an abort request. APIs such as fetch and timers/promises support signals. Custom or third-party APIs must explicitly cooperate or the underlying work can continue.

Combine caller cancellation with a timeout and keep the same signal through response-body consumption when needed. A timeout response does not imply a remote write was rolled back. Use idempotency for safe retries where the API supports it.
keyPoints: Share a total budget across attempts, and include backoff time in the budget.
Use the same total budget through retry scheduling and response-body reads, and record the difference between a deadline and caller cancellation.

blocks.title: Run as deadline.mjs
blocks.explanation: Use the same total budget through retry scheduling and response-body reads, and record the difference between a deadline and caller cancellation.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What is the difference between a timeout implemented with Promise.race and a signal?
blocks.answer: Promise.race can stop waiting for a result. A signal lets a supporting operation stop its work and clean up. A race alone does not notify the losing operation.
blocks.explanation: Use the same total budget through retry scheduling and response-body reads, and record the difference between a deadline and caller cancellation.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: If fetch resolves, is the complete response body already in memory?
blocks.answer: No. Fetch can resolve after the response headers arrive. Consuming the body can still take time or fail, so keep the relevant abort policy active while reading it.
hints: Distinguish headers from body consumption.
blocks.explanation:
Use the same total budget through retry scheduling and response-body reads, and record the difference between a deadline and caller cancellation.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/api/globals.html#class-abortsignal)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: An Angular page is closed while its BFF request waits for two upstream calls. What should the BFF do?
blocks.answer: Observe the downstream connection lifecycle, cancel supporting upstream calls when the result is no longer needed, and preserve a request deadline for calls that remain useful. Record cancellation separately from unexpected failures.
blocks.explanation: Share a total budget across attempts, and include backoff time in the budget.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Starting a fresh full timeout on every retry.
blocks.whyItHappens: Each individual attempt may fit its own limit, while combined attempts and backoff exceed the caller's deadline.
blocks.correctApproach: Share a total budget across attempts, and include backoff time in the budget.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Share a total budget across attempts, and include backoff time in the budget.

Use the same total budget through retry scheduling and response-body reads, and record the difference between a deadline and caller cancellation.

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.content:
Propagate request deadlines into asynchronous dependencies. Promise.race can stop waiting for a result. A signal lets a supporting operation stop its work and clean up. A race alone does not notify the losing operation.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/api/globals.html#class-abortsignal)

title: File I/O, Paths, and Resource Ownership
description: Read files reliably from modules and close handles on every path.

blocks.title: File I/O, Paths, and Resource Ownership
blocks.content:
Relative paths passed as strings to filesystem APIs are interpreted from the process working directory. Use a file URL relative to import.meta.url for a packaged asset and a configured absolute path for deployment data.

Read a bounded file with readFile or stream a large one. When you open a FileHandle yourself, give one scope responsibility for closing it. Close it in finally even if a read fails.
keyPoints: Respect bytesRead and define who closes the file handle.
The example reads a partial file into a fixed buffer. Its finally block represents the general cleanup contract.

blocks.title: Run as read-self.mjs
blocks.explanation: The example reads a partial file into a fixed buffer. Its finally block represents the general cleanup contract.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: When is readFile a reasonable choice?
blocks.answer: When the file is small enough for the configured memory budget and you need all its bytes before processing. Use a stream for bounded-memory processing of larger data.
blocks.explanation: The example reads a partial file into a fixed buffer. Its finally block represents the general cleanup contract.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Does changing the directory from which you launch node change a URL resolved from import.meta.url?
blocks.answer: No. The base URL identifies the current module. In contrast, a relative filesystem path like ./config.json depends on the working directory.
hints: Identify the base value for each path form.
blocks.explanation:
The example reads a partial file into a fixed buffer. Its finally block represents the general cleanup contract.

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: Reading a bundled configuration works locally but fails under a service manager. How do you diagnose it?
blocks.answer: Log the working directory and the resolved path without logging configuration contents. Decide whether the file is a packaged asset or an operator-provided config value, then resolve it from the appropriate fixed base.
blocks.explanation: Respect bytesRead and define who closes the file handle.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Assuming every read fills the requested buffer length.
blocks.whyItHappens: A read may return fewer bytes than requested, for example near EOF. Bytes outside the returned slice do not represent newly read data.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Respect bytesRead and define who closes the file handle.

The example reads a partial file into a fixed buffer. Its finally block represents the general cleanup contract.

title: Buffers, Encodings, and Shared Memory
description: Distinguish byte length from string length and copy from view.

blocks.title: Buffers, Encodings, and Shared Memory
blocks.content:
Buffers represent bytes. UTF-8 encodes some characters as more than one byte, and JavaScript string length counts UTF-16 code units. Use Buffer.byteLength for an encoded string and validate size in the unit the protocol expects.

Buffer.subarray gives a view over shared storage. Buffer.from(existingBuffer) copies its bytes. Decode arbitrarily split UTF-8 chunks through StringDecoder or a streaming TextDecoder to preserve incomplete characters.
keyPoints: Define byte limits explicitly and avoid retaining tiny views into large buffers for long periods.
Choose whether data ownership may be shared before handing a subarray to another component.

blocks.title: Run as buffers.mjs
blocks.explanation: Choose whether data ownership may be shared before handing a subarray to another component.

blocks.title: Predict the output
blocks.question: What number and JSON-quoted string does buffers.mjs print?
blocks.explanation: The euro sign takes three bytes in UTF-8. StringDecoder holds the incomplete leading byte until the remaining bytes arrive.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Why can decoding each chunk as UTF-8 independently corrupt text?
blocks.answer: A chunk may end in the middle of a multi-byte character. The next chunk has the remaining bytes. A streaming decoder retains the incomplete sequence until it can decode it.
blocks.explanation: Choose whether data ownership may be shared before handing a subarray to another component.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: If you mutate a Buffer.subarray result, can it change the original Buffer?
blocks.answer: Yes. Both values address the same underlying storage. Use Buffer.from(view) when the recipient needs an independent copy.
hints: Determine whether Node created a view or allocated new bytes.
blocks.explanation:
Choose whether data ownership may be shared before handing a subarray to another component.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/api/buffer.html)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: An HTTP export shows corrupted accented names only for large datasets. What do you check?
blocks.answer: Check that byte chunks are decoded incrementally before text parsing. Reproduce with a fixture that deliberately splits a multi-byte character across chunks and verify the export end to end.
blocks.explanation: Define byte limits explicitly and avoid retaining tiny views into large buffers for long periods.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Using string.length for a UTF-8 byte quota.
blocks.whyItHappens: JavaScript strings report UTF-16 code units, while protocol limits often measure encoded bytes.
blocks.correctApproach: Define byte limits explicitly and avoid retaining tiny views into large buffers for long periods.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Define byte limits explicitly and avoid retaining tiny views into large buffers for long periods.

Choose whether data ownership may be shared before handing a subarray to another component.

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.content:

title: Streams, Pipeline, and Backpressure
description: Compose readable, transform, and writable streams with bounded buffering.

blocks.title: Streams, Pipeline, and Backpressure
blocks.content:
A readable produces chunks, a transform converts them, and a writable consumes them. Backpressure tells a producer to slow down when a downstream stage cannot keep up. A manual call to write returns false once buffering crosses its threshold. Wait for drain before resuming production.

The promise-based pipeline coordinates backpressure, completion, and errors for connected streams. The highWaterMark is a buffering threshold. It cannot cap the memory in a pipeline that also accumulates data in application arrays or creates oversized chunks.
keyPoints: Propagate cancellation and use incremental producers with bounded input sizes.
Test pipeline behavior against a slow writable, input failure, and early cancellation.

blocks.title: Run as streams.mjs
blocks.explanation: Test pipeline behavior against a slow writable, input failure, and early cancellation.

blocks.title: Predict the output
blocks.question: Which two lines are written even though the sink is asynchronous?
blocks.answer:
A
B
blocks.explanation: The transform uppercases the input, and the writable handles each queued chunk in stream order.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Why is pipeline useful even when pipe already connects streams?
blocks.answer: Pipeline observes completion and propagates errors across the chain with cleanup. With manual piping, the caller has to coordinate error handling and completion for all stages.
blocks.explanation: Test pipeline behavior against a slow writable, input failure, and early cancellation.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Is highWaterMark a hard upper bound on memory for the whole pipeline?
blocks.answer: No. It is a buffering threshold on an individual stream. Transforms can buffer separately, a chunk can exceed the threshold, and object mode counts objects rather than their bytes.
hints: Account for every stage and its buffering unit.
blocks.explanation:
Test pipeline behavior against a slow writable, input failure, and early cancellation.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: A vehicle export climbs to gigabytes of RSS when several users download it. How do you redesign it?
blocks.answer: Use a paged or cursor-backed producer, incremental formatting, an abort-aware pipeline, and a global concurrency limit. Test with slow clients and track RSS, export completion rate, and cancellation.
blocks.explanation: Propagate cancellation and use incremental producers with bounded input sizes.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Accumulating all export rows before starting the stream.
blocks.whyItHappens: Returning a stream from the HTTP handler only reduces memory if upstream retrieval and transformations also avoid collecting all data.
blocks.correctApproach: Propagate cancellation and use incremental producers with bounded input sizes.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Propagate cancellation and use incremental producers with bounded input sizes.

Test pipeline behavior against a slow writable, input failure, and early cancellation.

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.content:
Compose readable, transform, and writable streams with bounded buffering. Pipeline observes completion and propagates errors across the chain with cleanup. With manual piping, the caller has to coordinate error handling and completion for all stages.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html)

title: HTTP Request Lifecycle and JSON Responses
description: Build a small HTTP handler and reason about headers, body, and completion.

blocks.title: HTTP Request Lifecycle and JSON Responses
blocks.content:
In Node's low-level HTTP API, IncomingMessage is a readable stream and ServerResponse writes headers and body to the connection. The handler runs once per request, which can share a TCP connection with other sequential requests.

Send headers before committing response content, and call end to finish the response. Apply limits and timeouts before parsing user-supplied request bodies. Handle incorrect methods and paths with appropriate HTTP status codes.
keyPoints: Apply body limits before parsing and define consistent JSON responses for expected failures.
For a production endpoint, align proxy and application timeouts and use an explicit body-size policy.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Which parts of an HTTP request do you have when the handler starts?
blocks.answer: The parsed request line and headers are available. The body is read from a stream and may continue to arrive over time.
blocks.explanation: For a production endpoint, align proxy and application timeouts and use an explicit body-size policy.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Can an error handler always replace a response with a new JSON error?
blocks.answer: Once headers have been sent, it is too late to change the status or content type. Use the stream error policy and signal a partially delivered response when the chosen protocol permits it.

blocks.answer: Set header and request timeouts, bound request-body size, and preserve proxy-level limits. Record which timeout expired and test a slow but legitimate upload so the new limits fit product behavior.

An error contract gives consumers a stable machine-readable code, an appropriate status, and optional safe details for presentation. RFC 9457 defines a standard problem-details representation for HTTP APIs. Report internal diagnostics through correlated logs.

Treat a schema failure and a business-rule failure as different cases when a client needs to respond differently.

title: Angular Backend for Frontend and Partial Failure

blocks.title: Angular Backend for Frontend and Partial Failure
blocks.content:
A backend for frontend adapts data and conventions for a particular interface. It can aggregate fleet telemetry, account state, and user preferences into a page model while keeping upstream request orchestration off the browser.

Classify each dependency as essential or optional. Run independent reads concurrently, apply individual deadlines under a total budget, and expose degradation explicitly. Share upstream results only when identity and entitlement rules allow it.
keyPoints: Define partial-failure semantics and draw a clear ownership boundary for domain rules.
An optional dependency's degraded response should be simple enough for the frontend to render consistently.

blocks.title: Interview question

blocks.explanation: An optional dependency's degraded response should be simple enough for the frontend to render consistently.

blocks.question: Should optional data timeout result in an empty list indistinguishable from an actual empty result?

blocks.question: Fleet warnings must load quickly even if preferences are slow. What would you ship?
blocks.answer: Treat fleet warnings and the user's authorization as essential. Give preferences a shorter independent budget and return a safe degraded preference state if needed. Measure dependency latency and enforce the total request deadline.

An optional dependency's degraded response should be simple enough for the frontend to render consistently.

title: Express Middleware and Error Handling
description: Compose middleware in request order and handle errors consistently in Express 5.

blocks.title: Express Middleware and Error Handling
blocks.content:
Express runs matching middleware in registration order. A handler responds, calls next to continue, or forwards an error. Put parsing and authentication before routes that require them, and place the error-handling middleware after routes.

Express 5 forwards rejections from promises returned by handlers. Work launched separately, such as a timer callback or a promise that was never returned, must report errors through its own lifecycle. Error middleware uses four arguments and delegates when headers have already been sent.
keyPoints: Give each path one response owner and test both expected errors and unexpected rejections.
Preserve the distinction between a synchronous throw, a returned promise rejection, and an independently scheduled callback.

blocks.title: Save as express-demo.mjs in a project with Express 5 installed
blocks.explanation: Preserve the distinction between a synchronous throw, a returned promise rejection, and an independently scheduled callback.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Why does error middleware accept four arguments even if it doesn't use all of them?
blocks.answer: Express identifies error-handling middleware by its four-argument signature. Keeping next also supports handing off errors after headers have been sent.
blocks.explanation: Preserve the distinction between a synchronous throw, a returned promise rejection, and an independently scheduled callback.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Does Express 5 automatically catch rejections from every promise started inside a handler?
blocks.answer: No. The framework can observe a returned or awaited promise through the handler's returned result. An independent promise chain needs its own supervision or explicit error forwarding.
hints: Ask which promise the framework can actually observe.
blocks.explanation:
Preserve the distinction between a synchronous throw, a returned promise rejection, and an independently scheduled callback.

[Further reading](https://expressjs.com/en/guide/error-handling.html)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: A new global parser makes upload requests fail before reaching their handlers. What do you inspect?
blocks.answer: Inspect middleware order, matching paths, request content type, body limits, and the actual upload format. Apply the parser only where needed and test JSON and upload routes separately.
blocks.explanation: Give each path one response owner and test both expected errors and unexpected rejections.

blocks.mistake: Calling next after sending a response and letting a second handler write headers.
blocks.whyItHappens: Sending a response does not stop arbitrary later code. Calling next explicitly advances the middleware chain.
blocks.correctApproach: Give each path one response owner and test both expected errors and unexpected rejections.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Give each path one response owner and test both expected errors and unexpected rejections.

Preserve the distinction between a synchronous throw, a returned promise rejection, and an independently scheduled callback.

blocks.content:

title: Database Pools and Transaction Boundaries
description: Tie related writes to one transaction and size database concurrency deliberately.

blocks.title: Database Pools and Transaction Boundaries
blocks.content:
A connection pool reuses database sessions. A transaction runs on one acquired connection from BEGIN through COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Separate pool.query calls may use different sessions. Use parameterized SQL and let database constraints guard shared invariants.

Pool size times the number of replicas determines the application's maximum allocated sessions. Keep transactions short and avoid slow remote calls inside them. For a transient serialization failure, rerun the complete transaction within a bounded retry policy when the operation allows it.
keyPoints: Release leased connections on every outcome and monitor pool queue time alongside query latency.
The example uses a test double. Confirm isolation and ambiguous commit outcomes against the actual database and driver.

blocks.explanation: The example uses a test double. Confirm isolation and ambiguous commit outcomes against the actual database and driver.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Why does each query in a transaction need the same connection?
blocks.answer: Transaction state is session-local. Acquiring a client once keeps each statement under that session's transaction and isolation context.
blocks.explanation: The example uses a test double. Confirm isolation and ambiguous commit outcomes against the actual database and driver.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Can pool.query('BEGIN') followed by several pool.query calls safely define a transaction?
blocks.answer: No. The pool is free to choose a different session for each query. Lease one client and release it after commit or rollback.
hints: Identify where database transaction state lives.
blocks.explanation:
The example uses a test double. Confirm isolation and ambiguous commit outcomes against the actual database and driver.

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: Two workers decrement the same inventory item concurrently. How do you maintain the invariant?
blocks.answer: Enforce the invariant atomically, for example with a conditional update plus a database constraint as appropriate. Check the affected row count and keep related writes inside the same transaction. Test concurrent attempts with the actual database.
blocks.explanation: Release leased connections on every outcome and monitor pool queue time alongside query latency.

blocks.mistake: Holding open a transaction while waiting on an unrelated remote service.

title: Idempotent Writes and Safe Retries
description: Design writes that tolerate an ambiguous response or a repeated request.

blocks.title: Idempotent Writes and Safe Retries
blocks.content:
An idempotency key identifies one logical request from a client. Scope it by principal and operation, store a fingerprint of the normalized request, and use an atomic uniqueness constraint to arbitrate competing attempts.

Model in-flight, completed, and expired records. Replay the completed outcome for the same fingerprint and define a conflict response for a mismatched payload. When effects cross storage systems, coordinate them with an outbox or the downstream provider's deduplication primitive.
keyPoints: Test duplicate arrivals, a timeout after commit, mismatched payloads, and expiry.
Keep the durable record long enough to cover the real retry window and scope keys by the correct principal.

blocks.title: Run as key-scope.mjs. This in-memory example only demonstrates composite key encoding.
blocks.explanation: Keep the durable record long enough to cover the real retry window and scope keys by the correct principal.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Which failures make idempotency especially valuable?
blocks.answer: A client timeout or disconnect can leave the caller unsure whether a write committed. Retrying with the same key lets the server discover the original outcome.
blocks.explanation: Keep the durable record long enough to cover the real retry window and scope keys by the correct principal.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Does a random key make a POST safe to retry if the client generates a new key on each attempt?
blocks.answer: No. A new key identifies a different logical request. The same key and equivalent payload must survive all retries for that operation.
hints: Count logical operations rather than network attempts.
blocks.explanation:
Keep the durable record long enough to cover the real retry window and scope keys by the correct principal.

[Further reading](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: Two pods receive the same create-export request at the same time. What guarantees one outcome?
blocks.answer: Acquire the key in a shared store with a unique constraint. Atomically bind the operation and stored result when possible. Return a documented response while processing is in flight and replay the recorded result when complete.
blocks.explanation: Test duplicate arrivals, a timeout after commit, mismatched payloads, and expiry.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Protecting against duplicates with an in-process Map across several replicas.
blocks.whyItHappens: Each process owns a different Map, and all entries are lost when the process restarts.
blocks.correctApproach: Test duplicate arrivals, a timeout after commit, mismatched payloads, and expiry.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Test duplicate arrivals, a timeout after commit, mismatched payloads, and expiry.

Keep the durable record long enough to cover the real retry window and scope keys by the correct principal.

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.content:
Design writes that tolerate an ambiguous response or a repeated request. A client timeout or disconnect can leave the caller unsure whether a write committed. Retrying with the same key lets the server discover the original outcome.

title: Background Jobs, Queues, and the Transactional Outbox
description: Move long-running work out of requests and reason about duplicate delivery.

blocks.title: Background Jobs, Queues, and the Transactional Outbox
blocks.content:
A long-running export can return 202 with a job ID and a status endpoint. Persist job ownership and progress so polling is safe. A queue separates admission from execution and lets workers retry eligible failures independently of the HTTP request.

Store an outbox row with a business update in the same database transaction when publication must follow commit. A relay can publish duplicate messages if it crashes after send and before recording success. Consumers must tolerate repeat deliveries.
keyPoints: Make retries observable with job IDs, attempt counts, queue age, and stable failure codes.
If work may be delivered more than once, ensure the durable side effect and its deduplication marker use a consistent commit boundary.

blocks.title: Run as outbox-demo.mjs. Arrays stand in for durable storage and a broker.
blocks.explanation: If work may be delivered more than once, ensure the durable side effect and its deduplication marker use a consistent commit boundary.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What should a client receive after submitting a long-running job?
blocks.answer: A stable job identifier and a way to read status. Document terminal states, authorization, retention, retry behavior, and any progress values the system can reliably report.
blocks.explanation: If work may be delivered more than once, ensure the durable side effect and its deduplication marker use a consistent commit boundary.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Does a transactional outbox guarantee that a consumer receives a message exactly once?
blocks.answer: No. It closes the gap between the database transaction and the durable intent to publish. The relay may publish more than once. Deduplicate consumer effects using a durable operation ID.
hints: Follow the crash window between publish and acknowledgement.
blocks.explanation:
If work may be delivered more than once, ensure the durable side effect and its deduplication marker use a consistent commit boundary.

[Further reading](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/transactional-outbox.html)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: An Excel export repeatedly fails and head-of-line retries delay every other export. How do you recover?
blocks.answer: Use bounded attempts with backoff and jitter for transient errors, record terminal failure separately, and isolate jobs that cannot succeed. Limit per-tenant and global concurrency, and monitor queue age and repeat failure causes.
blocks.explanation: Make retries observable with job IDs, attempt counts, queue age, and stable failure codes.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Marking a message processed before its durable effect is committed.
blocks.whyItHappens: A crash after marking but before committing can make the next delivery appear complete when the effect never happened.
blocks.correctApproach: Make retries observable with job IDs, attempt counts, queue age, and stable failure codes.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Make retries observable with job IDs, attempt counts, queue age, and stable failure codes.

If work may be delivered more than once, ensure the durable side effect and its deduplication marker use a consistent commit boundary.

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.content:
Move long-running work out of requests and reason about duplicate delivery. A stable job identifier and a way to read status. Document terminal states, authorization, retention, retry behavior, and any progress values the system can reliably report.

[Further reading](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/transactional-outbox.html)

title: Caching, Cache Keys, and Concurrent Misses
description: Design cache policy around identity, expiry, and load bursts.

blocks.title: Caching, Cache Keys, and Concurrent Misses
blocks.content:
Choose a cache key that includes every dimension that affects the result, such as tenant, resource, locale, or a permission-sensitive variant. Define maximum staleness and invalidate writes whose results need immediate visibility.

A popular key can generate concurrent misses when it expires. Combine compatible in-flight reads inside a process and apply a separate policy for distributed coordination if needed. Avoid caching rejected in-flight promises indefinitely.
keyPoints: Write down staleness and key-scope rules, and test cross-tenant reads alongside concurrent misses.
When refreshes are shared, verify the keys contain the entire scope that determines whether a result is reusable.

blocks.title: Run as single-flight.mjs. This coalesces overlapping fetches inside one process only.
blocks.explanation: When refreshes are shared, verify the keys contain the entire scope that determines whether a result is reusable.

blocks.title: Predict the output
blocks.question: What array does single-flight.mjs print, and how many times is load called?
blocks.answer: [1, 1], with a single invocation of load.
blocks.explanation: Both requests overlap on the same key and receive the same pending promise. The finally callback removes the entry after the result settles.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: How does single-flight differ from result caching?
blocks.answer: Single-flight shares work while a compatible request is already in progress. A result cache serves later requests from a completed value until invalidation or expiry.
blocks.explanation: When refreshes are shared, verify the keys contain the entire scope that determines whether a result is reusable.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Does an in-process promise map prevent a cache stampede across all service replicas?
blocks.answer: No. Each process has its own map. Distributed coordination or a suitable shared cache policy is needed when the upstream cannot handle one load per replica.
hints: Identify the scope of the Map.
blocks.explanation:
When refreshes are shared, verify the keys contain the entire scope that determines whether a result is reusable.

[Further reading](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cache-aside)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: A fleet summary cache causes a read surge every minute. How do you diagnose it?
blocks.answer: Correlate upstream traffic with key expiry, then measure cache hit rate and per-key refresh concurrency. Consider coalescing, randomized expiry, or safe stale reads while refreshing. Verify freshness and tenant isolation under load.
blocks.explanation: Write down staleness and key-scope rules, and test cross-tenant reads alongside concurrent misses.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Sharing cached answers across accounts because the route is identical.
blocks.whyItHappens: A common URL can produce different results for different requesters. A key that omits those differences makes an unsafe cache entry reusable.
blocks.correctApproach: Write down staleness and key-scope rules, and test cross-tenant reads alongside concurrent misses.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Write down staleness and key-scope rules, and test cross-tenant reads alongside concurrent misses.

When refreshes are shared, verify the keys contain the entire scope that determines whether a result is reusable.

blocks.content:
Design cache policy around identity, expiry, and load bursts. Single-flight shares work while a compatible request is already in progress. A result cache serves later requests from a completed value until invalidation or expiry.

title: Worker Threads and Transferable Data
description: Offload independent CPU-heavy work and choose a data-transfer strategy.

blocks.title: Worker Threads and Transferable Data
blocks.content:
Each worker thread executes JavaScript in its own V8 isolate. Workers are useful for CPU-intensive JavaScript. Node's regular asynchronous I/O APIs already offer a way to avoid blocking on I/O without assigning a worker to every request.

Messages use structured clone by default. Transferring an owned ArrayBuffer moves its backing storage and detaches the sender's buffer. SharedArrayBuffer allows access from multiple threads and needs explicit synchronization for shared mutations. A bounded pool amortizes initialization and controls load.
keyPoints: Set worker and queue bounds so oversubscription remains predictable under load.
An owned ArrayBuffer is suitable for transfer. Pooled Buffers can follow different cloning behavior.

blocks.title: Run as worker-demo.mjs
blocks.explanation: An owned ArrayBuffer is suitable for transfer. Pooled Buffers can follow different cloning behavior.

blocks.title: Predict the output
blocks.question: What are the two lines printed by the main thread?
blocks.answer:
detached length: 0
sum: 6
blocks.explanation: The backing buffer is detached as soon as it is transferred. The worker sums the bytes in its own isolate and sends the result back later.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: When is a worker thread a good fit?
blocks.answer: When CPU-heavy JavaScript can run independently and transfer plus scheduling costs are acceptable. Compare wall time, main-thread delay, and queue pressure under realistic load.
blocks.explanation: An owned ArrayBuffer is suitable for transfer. Pooled Buffers can follow different cloning behavior.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Can the sender continue reading a normal ArrayBuffer after transferring it?
blocks.answer: No. Transferring detaches the backing store from the sender. A structured clone copies data, while a SharedArrayBuffer uses shared storage and different coordination rules.
hints: Separate moving ownership from copying or sharing bytes.
blocks.explanation:
An owned ArrayBuffer is suitable for transfer. Pooled Buffers can follow different cloning behavior.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/api/worker_threads.html)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: A JSON transformation takes 200 ms and blocks every request on a pod. What changes?
blocks.answer: Benchmark smaller incremental transforms and a bounded worker pool. Test transfer costs, queue length, timeouts, and behavior on worker failure. If this work must survive restarts, persist it as a background job.
blocks.explanation: Set worker and queue bounds so oversubscription remains predictable under load.

blocks.mistake: Starting a new Worker for every small request.
blocks.whyItHappens: Creating a worker requires initialization, memory, and coordination. The overhead can exceed the value of a small job.
blocks.correctApproach: Set worker and queue bounds so oversubscription remains predictable under load.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Set worker and queue bounds so oversubscription remains predictable under load.

An owned ArrayBuffer is suitable for transfer. Pooled Buffers can follow different cloning behavior.

title: Child Processes, IPC, and Isolation
description: Choose an execution boundary and handle child process completion reliably.

blocks.title: Child Processes, IPC, and Isolation
blocks.content:
A child process has a separate process lifetime and address space. Use spawn with an argument array when running a known executable and streaming output. exec generally launches a shell and buffers output. fork is a Node-specific child process helper with an IPC channel.

Handle spawn errors and wait for close if the output must be fully consumed. Keep executable choice and argument types controlled. Distinguish launch failure, nonzero exit, cancellation, and a timed-out operation in the parent.
keyPoints: Pass controlled arguments directly, observe completion, and cap any collected output.
Local process separation supports isolation and lifecycle ownership, but it is insufficient by itself for executing untrusted programs.

blocks.title: Run as child-demo.mjs
blocks.explanation: Local process separation supports isolation and lifecycle ownership, but it is insufficient by itself for executing untrusted programs.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: How do spawn and fork differ?
blocks.answer: spawn starts an executable with configurable stdio. fork starts another Node process and includes an IPC channel for structured messages.
blocks.explanation: Local process separation supports isolation and lifecycle ownership, but it is insufficient by itself for executing untrusted programs.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Does a child's exit event mean the parent has consumed all piped output?
blocks.answer: Not necessarily. Wait for close to know that the child's stdio streams have closed. Handle application-level output completion as well if data is being transformed or written elsewhere.
hints: Track process lifetime and stream lifetime separately.
blocks.explanation:
Local process separation supports isolation and lifecycle ownership, but it is insufficient by itself for executing untrusted programs.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/api/child_process.html)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: A CLI report tool sometimes never returns and workers pile up. How would you contain the impact?
blocks.answer: Add a job deadline, bounded child concurrency, a kill policy, and output limits. Record exit code or signal, drain output on normal completion, and verify timeout handling through a test fixture.
blocks.explanation: Pass controlled arguments directly, observe completion, and cap any collected output.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Waiting only for a successful exit and ignoring process startup errors.
blocks.whyItHappens: A child can fail to spawn before an exit code is available. The parent needs an error path for that event.
blocks.correctApproach: Pass controlled arguments directly, observe completion, and cap any collected output.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Pass controlled arguments directly, observe completion, and cap any collected output.

Local process separation supports isolation and lifecycle ownership, but it is insufficient by itself for executing untrusted programs.

Choose an execution boundary and handle child process completion reliably. spawn starts an executable with configurable stdio. fork starts another Node process and includes an IPC channel for structured messages.

title: libuv Thread Pool Contention
description: Identify pool-backed work and separate thread-pool delay from a blocked event loop.

blocks.title: libuv Thread Pool Contention
blocks.content:
Selected filesystem, crypto, compression, and DNS operations use libuv's shared worker pool. Most socket readiness notifications use operating-system mechanisms. A process can have a responsive main thread while pool-backed file work queues behind expensive jobs.

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE is a startup configuration. Increasing it has CPU and memory costs and cannot fix arbitrary synchronous JavaScript. First measure latency in pool-backed operations and bound the rate of expensive tasks.
keyPoints: Set and measure pool configuration at process startup and control expensive work at admission.
The demo illustrates possible queueing. Scheduling and timings vary with hardware, concurrency, and startup configuration.

blocks.explanation: The demo illustrates possible queueing. Scheduling and timings vary with hardware, concurrency, and startup configuration.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What telemetry helps distinguish a busy event loop from pool contention?
blocks.answer: Compare event-loop delay, process CPU, and latency of specific operations. Add queue and concurrency metrics around expensive application work, then profile if the source remains unclear.
blocks.explanation: The demo illustrates possible queueing. Scheduling and timings vary with hardware, concurrency, and startup configuration.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Will increasing UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE speed up synchronous JSON.parse on the main thread?
blocks.answer: No. JSON.parse runs synchronously on the JavaScript thread. A pool size change only influences operations that use the libuv pool.

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: File reads slow down when many password hashes run. What is your first experiment?
blocks.answer: Repeat the workload with capped hash concurrency and track file latency, hash throughput, CPU, and loop delay. Compare with isolating CPU-heavy jobs. Tune pool sizing only after the measurements distinguish queueing from resource limits.
blocks.explanation: Set and measure pool configuration at process startup and control expensive work at admission.

blocks.whyItHappens: The pool may already exist when application code starts. The runtime does not resize it as a general reaction to changing process.env.
blocks.correctApproach: Set and measure pool configuration at process startup and control expensive work at admission.

title: Node Test Runner, HTTP Tests, and Isolation
description: Write deterministic unit and HTTP tests with clear resource ownership.

blocks.title: Node Test Runner, HTTP Tests, and Isolation
blocks.content:
The node:test runner executes tests written with standard Node APIs. Use node:assert/strict for assertions and await asynchronous work. For an HTTP integration test, bind an ephemeral port and register server cleanup before exercising the request.

Inject external adapters so unit tests can replace them. Use real integration tests for boundaries where semantics matter, such as a transaction or a response contract. Avoid testing timing through arbitrary sleep intervals.
keyPoints: Await readiness and cleanup explicitly, and exercise error paths alongside successful requests.
The endpoint test awaits both server readiness and client completion, then closes the listener.

blocks.title: Save as health.test.mjs and run node --test health.test.mjs
blocks.explanation: The endpoint test awaits both server readiness and client completion, then closes the listener.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Why use port zero in integration tests?
blocks.answer: The operating system chooses a free port. Parallel tests avoid collisions with a hard-coded port, and the test reads the assigned port after listening.
blocks.explanation: The endpoint test awaits both server readiness and client completion, then closes the listener.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Can a test callback return before an assertion inside a later promise and still reliably fail on that assertion?
blocks.answer: No. The runner has no way to treat unawaited work as the test's normal result. Return or await the promise so assertion failures are attributed to the test.
hints: Identify what the test runner actually awaits.
blocks.explanation:
The endpoint test awaits both server readiness and client completion, then closes the listener.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/api/test.html)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: HTTP tests pass one at a time and fail under CI parallelism. Where do you look first?
blocks.answer: Inspect shared ports, global state, environment variables, reused fixtures, and unclosed clients. Give each test control of its dependencies and use registered teardown to return shared resources.
blocks.explanation: Await readiness and cleanup explicitly, and exercise error paths alongside successful requests.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Sleeping for 500 ms rather than awaiting the server's readiness event.
blocks.whyItHappens: A fixed sleep can be too short under load and wastes time in fast runs. A readiness event expresses the actual dependency.
blocks.correctApproach: Await readiness and cleanup explicitly, and exercise error paths alongside successful requests.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Await readiness and cleanup explicitly, and exercise error paths alongside successful requests.

The endpoint test awaits both server readiness and client completion, then closes the listener.

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.content:
Write deterministic unit and HTTP tests with clear resource ownership. The operating system chooses a free port. Parallel tests avoid collisions with a hard-coded port, and the test reads the assigned port after listening.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/api/test.html)

title: Request Context with AsyncLocalStorage
description: Correlate asynchronous work without a mutable global request ID.

blocks.title: Request Context with AsyncLocalStorage
blocks.content:
AsyncLocalStorage associates a store with work started inside run. Awaited tasks created there generally see the same store. Start a separate context for each request. Capture a small set of identifiers instead of retaining complete request objects.

Use correlation IDs to connect internal logs. Distributed trace propagation is a separate concern spanning network boundaries. Shared mutable objects stored in a context can still be mutated by multiple operations within that same request.
keyPoints: Use run at the request boundary and keep the stored correlation data small and free of secrets.
For a distributed trace, propagate the appropriate trace metadata to upstream calls separately from local context.

blocks.title: Run as context-demo.mjs
blocks.explanation: For a distributed trace, propagate the appropriate trace metadata to upstream calls separately from local context.

blocks.title: Predict the output
blocks.question: What IDs appear inside the two callbacks, and what does the final line print?
blocks.answer: Each callback logs its own ID, fleet-a or fleet-b. The final line is undefined.
blocks.explanation: The callbacks execute in separate async contexts. The outer code has no active store.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Why shouldn't you use a module-level currentRequestId variable?
blocks.answer: Concurrent requests interleave around awaits and overwrite shared state. Request context scopes identifiers to the async operations belonging to that request.
blocks.explanation: For a distributed trace, propagate the appropriate trace metadata to upstream calls separately from local context.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Will getStore always return a store anywhere in the process after the first call to run?
blocks.answer: No. It returns the context active for the current execution. Code outside those contexts sees undefined unless another context was installed.
hints: Trace the async ancestry of the call site.
blocks.explanation:
For a distributed trace, propagate the appropriate trace metadata to upstream calls separately from local context.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/api/async_context.html)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: One request loses its ID when an adapter calls back. How do you debug it?
blocks.answer: Reproduce the failing boundary in isolation and check the store before adapter registration and inside the callback. Verify context propagation and bind or bridge integrations that don't preserve it, then test simultaneous requests.
blocks.explanation: Use run at the request boundary and keep the stored correlation data small and free of secrets.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Using request IDs as authorization evidence.
blocks.whyItHappens: A request ID is metadata for correlation. It may come from an untrusted source and does not establish access.
blocks.correctApproach: Use run at the request boundary and keep the stored correlation data small and free of secrets.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Use run at the request boundary and keep the stored correlation data small and free of secrets.

title: Event-Loop Metrics, CPU Profiles, and Memory
description: Choose measurements that distinguish CPU stalls, leaks, and dependency latency.

blocks.title: Event-Loop Metrics, CPU Profiles, and Memory
blocks.content:
Event-loop delay measures how late the loop can service scheduled work. Event-loop utilization measures active versus idle time over an interval. Neither identifies the blocking function by itself. Compare CPU profiles, GC activity, and upstream span timings under similar load.

Use process.memoryUsage to compare heap, external allocations, and RSS. Buffers contribute to external memory and RSS, so a stable V8 heap does not rule out rising process memory. Capture snapshots only where their overhead and confidentiality can be managed.
keyPoints: Measure p95 and p99 request latency, loop delay, and memory over the same interval.
Profile at the same load where the symptom appears. A single process-wide number cannot identify the function or dependency by itself.

blocks.title: Run as perf-demo.mjs. The controlled busy loop simulates blocking.
blocks.explanation: Profile at the same load where the symptom appears. A single process-wide number cannot identify the function or dependency by itself.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: How do you tell an upstream dependency is slow when the event loop is healthy?
blocks.answer: Compare request span duration to upstream phases and pool queue time. If expensive waiting is visible in upstream spans while event-loop delay and CPU are flat, investigate the dependency, connectivity, and resource pools.
blocks.explanation: Profile at the same load where the symptom appears. A single process-wide number cannot identify the function or dependency by itself.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: Does a stable heapUsed value prove there is no growing memory footprint?
blocks.answer: No. External allocations, retained Buffers, worker isolates, or allocator behavior can affect RSS without the same change to heapUsed.
hints: Compare what heapUsed measures with what the process RSS includes.
blocks.explanation:
Profile at the same load where the symptom appears. A single process-wide number cannot identify the function or dependency by itself.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/api/perf_hooks.html)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: After Excel exports, a pod's RSS rises but the heap appears stable. Where do you start?
blocks.answer: Track RSS, external memory, arrayBuffers, concurrency, and export completion against a repeatable run. Check buffer retention and downstream backpressure. Use a memory or allocation profile appropriate to the suspected layer.
blocks.explanation: Measure p95 and p99 request latency, loop delay, and memory over the same interval.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Tuning flags before capturing metrics on a repeatable workload.
blocks.whyItHappens: Changing runtime settings before measuring makes it hard to distinguish improvements from load variation.
blocks.correctApproach: Measure p95 and p99 request latency, loop delay, and memory over the same interval.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Measure p95 and p99 request latency, loop delay, and memory over the same interval.

Profile at the same load where the symptom appears. A single process-wide number cannot identify the function or dependency by itself.

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.content:
Choose measurements that distinguish CPU stalls, leaks, and dependency latency. Compare request span duration to upstream phases and pool queue time. If expensive waiting is visible in upstream spans while event-loop delay and CPU are flat, investigate the dependency, connectivity, and resource pools.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/api/perf_hooks.html)

title: Running TypeScript and Checking Types
description: Distinguish executing TypeScript files from checking their types.

blocks.title: Running TypeScript and Checking Types
blocks.content:
Recent Node releases can execute TypeScript files using built-in type stripping for supported erasable syntax. That removes annotations before execution. It does not run the TypeScript checker or use tsconfig.json to transform syntax or resolve import aliases.

Use a supported Node 24 environment for the example. Run tsc with noEmit in CI when relying on direct execution. Projects that need compiler transforms, bundling, declarations, or alias rewriting should explicitly choose a build or supported loader.
keyPoints: Document one supported execution path and verify it together with the type check in CI.
Node infers the module format of TypeScript extensions using its runtime rules. Use .mts or .cts when explicitly required.

blocks.title: Save as score.ts and run node score.ts on Node 24
blocks.explanation: Node infers the module format of TypeScript extensions using its runtime rules. Use .mts or .cts when explicitly required.

blocks.title: Predict the output
blocks.question: What value does score.ts print?
blocks.explanation: The runtime erases the type annotations. The resulting JavaScript divides 7 by 10 and multiplies by 100.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: When do you still need a TypeScript compiler or checker?
blocks.answer: Use a checker to enforce type correctness. Use an appropriate build pipeline when you need emitted JavaScript, declarations, transform-dependent syntax, or bundle output.
blocks.explanation: Node infers the module format of TypeScript extensions using its runtime rules. Use .mts or .cts when explicitly required.

blocks.title: Tricky question
blocks.question: If node index.ts runs successfully, can CI assume the code type-checks?
blocks.answer: No. Stripping annotations does not verify their correctness. Run tsc --noEmit or your project's type-checking command explicitly.
hints: Separate runtime execution from static analysis.
blocks.explanation:
Node infers the module format of TypeScript extensions using its runtime rules. Use .mts or .cts when explicitly required.

[Further reading](https://nodejs.org/api/typescript.html)

blocks.title: Production scenario
blocks.question: An Angular developer reuses a tsconfig path alias in a Node service and gets a module resolution error. What is the fix?
blocks.answer: Choose a resolver that understands the project setup, use a Node-native package imports mapping where appropriate, or use explicit relative imports. Test the emitted or directly executable files in the same mode used in production.
blocks.explanation: Document one supported execution path and verify it together with the type check in CI.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Assuming Node's type stripping reads and applies every tsconfig option.
blocks.whyItHappens: Type stripping is deliberately narrower than a TypeScript project build, so compile-time aliases or transformations may fail at runtime.
blocks.correctApproach: Document one supported execution path and verify it together with the type check in CI.

blocks.title: Best practice
blocks.content:
Document one supported execution path and verify it together with the type check in CI.

Node infers the module format of TypeScript extensions using its runtime rules. Use .mts or .cts when explicitly required.

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.content:
Distinguish executing TypeScript files from checking their types. Use a checker to enforce type correctness. Use an appropriate build pipeline when you need emitted JavaScript, declarations, transform-dependent syntax, or bundle output.
